strengths: The paper addresses a useful deployment problem: serving previously unseen federated clients without labeled fine-tuning. Client-level expert selection followed by sample-level routing provides a coherent approach to this setting.

Anchor-client supervision offers a plausible mechanism for stabilizing expert specialization while communicating only selected experts. The objectives, system diagram, and pseudocode make the main algorithm understandable.

The reported improvements are substantial in the evaluated settings: Table 1 reaches 95.7% on CIFAR10 and 78.6% on CIFAR100; initializing experts from the common model increases CIFAR100 accuracy to 83.27% in Table 2.

The ablations examine meaningful dependencies, including pretrained-model quality, anchor sampling, expert initialization, overlapping anchor labels, and changing client pools. Reporting failure cases provides useful information about the method’s operating conditions.
weaknesses: The baseline results do not convincingly establish the claimed superiority. In Table 1, CIFAR10 FedAvg falls from a 73% pretrained starting point to 31.2%, while SCAFFOLD reaches chance accuracy. Appendix B.1 acknowledges a learning-rate mismatch, but tuning ranges and selected configurations are not documented. Although baseline failure does not itself invalidate FedJETs, these unusually weak comparisons require stronger optimization controls and validation-based model selection.

Practical applicability depends on restrictive conditions. The main setup constructs anchors with disjoint label groups and allocates half of each round to them; all five CIFAR10 anchors consequently participate every round. The overlapping-anchor experiment is useful, but availability and representativeness remain untested. Performance also depends sharply on common-expert quality. Evaluation on two CIFAR datasets with synthetic label shifts does not establish robustness to broader client distribution shifts or small incoming unlabeled batches.

The experiments do not sufficiently isolate the proposed specialization mechanism. Anchor supervision and oversampling change together, and there are no matched random-routing, fixed-routing, or anchor-only controls. Appendix D does not clearly define what constitutes a correct routing decision; its 27.1% CIFAR100 error rate does not substantiate the claim of near-perfect expert selection.

Originality relative to prior federated mixture and multitask learning is insufficiently established. Most components are standard, making a precise account of the additional contribution essential. Relevant approaches such as FedEM are not discussed or evaluated. Appendix H’s k-means visualization cannot justify dismissing methods that model clients as mixtures of underlying distributions.

The efficiency claims lack end-to-end evidence. Selecting K rather than M experts clearly reduces transmission relative to sending the entire same-sized pool, but the main comparison uses two FedMix experts versus five or ten FedJETs experts. Appendix F’s matched-expert comparisons use K=M and therefore do not validate sparse communication at matched capacity. Communication bytes, runtime, memory, and preprocessing/inference costs are not measured.

Reproducibility and statistical support are inadequate. The exact common-model pretraining procedure and data splits, client sample counts, router dimensions, normalization handling, and baseline tuning values are insufficiently specified. No independent-run uncertainty estimates or implementation link are provided. Several appendix tables report the best test accuracy across evaluations without describing a separate validation selection protocol.

Some claims exceed the evidence. Describing the method as agnostic to common-expert performance conflicts with its demonstrated sensitivity. Likewise, retaining raw data locally does not establish the unconditional privacy claim: expert identities and model updates are communicated without a stated threat model or privacy analysis. These are claim-calibration issues, rather than evidence of a serious ethical violation.
